passage: In the sixth-floor flat, Lokesh slid his blue counter two squares ahead while Baljeet went to fetch water. Baljeet came back, frowned at the board, and said, "Hey, it was here." Lokesh's face went hot and he wanted to run to the bedroom and hide under the bed. Mummy came and knelt down. "Did you move it?" He nodded, eyes wet. "Thank you for telling me. Can you say sorry to Baljeet and put it back? Then we can play again fairly." Lokesh whispered sorry, put the counter back, and Baljeet handed him the dice.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do while Baljeet was away?
qa.a: Lokesh slid his blue counter two squares ahead.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Baljeet frowned at the board?
qa.a: Lokesh felt ashamed. His hot face and wish to run to the bedroom and hide show it.

qa.q: How did Mummy help, and why was it better than calling Lokesh a bad child?
qa.a: Mummy asked calmly, thanked him for telling her, and helped him say sorry and play again fairly. A bad-child label might make him cheat better or stop playing. 🙂

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when the counter was moved?
qa.a: Baljeet was probably confused and a bit upset that the board had changed. Handing over the dice suggests he was ready to play again once Lokesh said sorry.

grounding: A child caught cheating feels hot-faced shame and wants to run away, and a wise adult helps him say sorry and try again fairly without calling him bad.

passage: Under the mango tree, Jeevan drew a circle in the dust for marbles. "New rule," he said. "Whoever shoots second loses." Rashmi always had to shoot second. He won every round. Her fists clenched and her face turned red. She wanted to throw the marbles into the well. Instead she said, "That is not fair, Jeevan!" He laughed. So she marched into the kitchen. "Amma, please come." Amma wiped her hands and said, "Jeevan, sometimes let the small one win. That is kind." Jeevan grumbled, then let Rashmi shoot first.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan draw the circle for marbles?
qa.a: Jeevan drew the circle in the dust under the mango tree.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling as Jeevan kept winning?
qa.a: Rashmi felt angry and powerless. Her clenched fists and red face show it, and she even wanted to throw the marbles into the well.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that helped, and what did Amma add?
qa.a: Rashmi said, "That is not fair," and asked Amma for help. Amma told Jeevan that letting the small one win sometimes is kind. 🙂

qa.q: How might Jeevan see the rule he made up?
qa.a: Jeevan may enjoy winning and not realise how it feels for Rashmi. He laughed at first and only grumbled when Amma spoke, so he may need to learn to see it from her side.

grounding: An older brother makes up rules that always let him win; the younger sister feels angry and powerless, says it is not fair and asks a parent for help.

passage: Note by Pooja, Irfan's mother. At Chacha's visit today, Irfan tore the wrapping and found grey socks, not the toy he hoped for. His face dropped and his shoulders slumped. I whispered, "Say thank you first." He mumbled, "Thank you, Chacha," and looked at the floor. Later in the car his lip shook and he cried, saying, "I wanted a car." I held him and said, "That is allowed. Chacha chose these because he thought of you, and that is his love." He sniffled, then asked if he could wear them tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Irfan find in the box?
qa.a: Irfan found grey socks, not the toy he hoped for.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he opened the gift?
qa.a: Irfan was disappointed and sad. His face dropped, his shoulders slumped, and he cried later in the car.

qa.q: What could a parent do to help a child with a disappointing gift?
qa.a: The parent can ask the child to say thank you first, and then let the child cry about it privately. The parent can explain that the gift shows the giver's love.

qa.q: How might Chacha have felt when Irfan said thank you and looked at the floor?
qa.a: Chacha may have noticed the small face and wondered whether Irfan liked it. Irfan's thank you still showed that he tried to be polite.

grounding: A child opens socks instead of a toy and looks disappointed, thanks the giver first, cries later, and the parent teaches the gift is someone's love.

passage: The living room was packed with guests and the cake was about to be cut when Ujjwal tore open Kishore Mama's parcel. Inside was a notebook. "I don't like this," he said loudly. "I wanted a car." A few people turned. Kishore Mama's smile wobbled. Mummy crouched and said quietly, "Say, 'Thank you, it was kind of you.'" Ujjwal repeated it to Mama. Later, as Mummy tucked him in, she asked, "What did you feel when you opened it?" "Sad," said Ujjwal. "Thank you for telling me," she said.

qa.q: What was inside Kishore Mama's parcel?
qa.a: A notebook was inside.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when he said, "I don't like this"?
qa.a: Ujjwal was disappointed and simply said what he felt. He was not trying to be rude, since he told Mummy later that he was sad.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Ujjwal in two steps?
qa.a: First she quietly gave him kind words to say to Kishore Mama, "Thank you, it was kind of you." Later at bedtime she asked him about his real feeling and listened.

qa.q: How might Kishore Mama have felt when Ujjwal spoke loudly?
qa.a: Kishore Mama probably felt a little hurt, since his smile wobbled. He may still understand that a small child says what he feels.

grounding: A child says "I don't like this" aloud to the gift-giver, a parent shows kind words afterwards and hears his real feeling later.

passage: Rain drummed on the roof as Vinita shook out her umbrella and handed over a gift bag. She had carried it on two buses. Tejas pulled out a green sweater and wrinkled up his nose. "Yuck," he said. Vinita felt a small sting, and her smile went stiff. His father started to scold, but Vinita touched his arm. "He's five. He shows what's on his face." Then his father said lightly, "Tejas, Vinita Aunty carried this through the rain. What do we say?" Tejas peeked up. "Thank you, Aunty."

qa.q: How did Vinita reach Tejas's house with the gift?
qa.a: She carried it on two buses through the rain.

qa.q: What did Vinita feel when Tejas wrinkled his nose at the sweater?
qa.a: Vinita felt a small sting of hurt. Her smile went stiff, but she understood that small children do not hide their feelings.

qa.q: How could a parent handle this without scolding?
qa.a: The father can say it lightly, reminding Tejas that Vinita carried the gift through the rain and asking what to say. That teaches gratitude without shaming.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been thinking when he said "Yuck"?
qa.a: Tejas was probably just showing his first reaction. He may have wanted a toy, not a sweater, and did not think about how it would land with Vinita.

grounding: A child makes a face at a gift and the giver feels sad but understands that small children do not hide feelings, while a wise adult reminds him lightly about gratitude.

passage: Rafiq sat at the little desk in the flat, tongue between his teeth, folding a sheet of paper into a card. He drew a big yellow cake with five candles and wrote V-I-N-I-T-A in wobbly red letters. Some glitter fell on the floor. On Saturday he walked into Vinita's birthday party in the colony hall, holding the card behind his back. His heart skipped with excitement. "Happy birthday!" he said, with a huge smile, and held it out. Vinita's eyes went wide as she looked at the cake.

qa.q: How many candles did Rafiq draw on the cake?
qa.a: Rafiq drew five candles.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling as he handed Vinita the card?
qa.a: Rafiq was excited and hoped Vinita would like it. His heart skipped and he gave a huge smile.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's card show about giving a gift?
qa.a: It shows that love can be in the effort, not the price. Rafiq folded, drew and wrote the card by himself. 🎉

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when she sees the card?
qa.a: Vinita may feel surprised and happy. Her wide eyes suggest she noticed the big yellow cake made for her.

grounding: A child draws a card for a friend's birthday and gives it with a big smile, excited that they will like it, showing love in the effort.

passage:
"Here, Sabina. I drew this for you," said Bhupen, pushing a paper across the bench.
"A dog! And a purple sky!" Sabina smiled wide. "Thank you, I love it!" She hugged it against her chest.
"It's Biscuit. He's my dog."
"Can I keep him at my house?"
"Yes, he can visit."
Sabina's cheeks felt warm. "I'll draw you something tomorrow. A big one."
"With a rainbow?"
"With a rainbow and me and you."

qa.q: What did Bhupen draw for Sabina?
qa.a: Bhupen drew a dog with a purple sky.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel after getting the drawing?
qa.a: Sabina felt loved and happy, and wanted to give something back. She hugged the paper and promised to draw one tomorrow.

qa.q: How did Sabina's way of saying thanks help their friendship?
qa.a: She said thank you kindly and hugged the drawing, so Bhupen could see it mattered. Then she planned to give a gift in return, which keeps the friendship warm. 😊

qa.q: What might Bhupen have felt when Sabina hugged his drawing?
qa.a: Bhupen was probably happy and proud that his friend loved it. He answered her warmly by saying the dog could visit.

grounding: A friend gives a drawing, the child says thank you I love it and hugs it, feeling loved and wanting to give back.

passage: On Sunday, Devika folded a paper in half, drew a red heart with a lopsided flower, and wrote PAPA in crayon. She gave it to him after breakfast. Papa smiled, said "Wow," and stuck it to the fridge with a mango-shaped magnet. Devika felt her chest puff up. On Monday morning she stood on tiptoe beside the fridge and pointed. "That is mine," she told Mummy Manjula. On Wednesday, when a neighbour visited, Papa said, "Look, Devika made that." Devika grinned and ran to fetch the crayons for another card.

qa.q: What did Papa use to stick the card to the fridge?
qa.a: Papa stuck it to the fridge with a mango-shaped magnet.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling on Monday morning when she pointed at the fridge?
qa.a: Devika felt proud that her card was there. She stood on tiptoe and said, "That is mine."

qa.q: What did Papa's actions teach Devika about giving?
qa.a: By putting the card on the fridge and showing it to the neighbour, Papa showed that her gift is valued. That tells Devika that her own effort matters. 🙂

qa.q: How might Papa feel every time he sees the card on the fridge?
qa.a: Papa probably feels happy and touched. He chose to show it to a visitor, which suggests he treasures it.

grounding: A child gives Papa a card, he puts it on the fridge, and over the following days she feels proud, learning that giving is valued.

passage: Priscila's cheeks were hot and her arms felt like wet noodles. She lay in bed under the yellow blanket in the flat in Lisbon, too tired to lift her teddy. Mummy Jana came in, put a cool hand on her forehead, and sat on the edge of the bed. "I'm right here," she said. Priscila curled up against her side. Mummy stroked her hair and hummed a little tune. The room was quiet. "You can rest," Mummy said. "You don't have to do anything." Priscila closed her eyes, small and warm and safe.

qa.q: Whose hand was on Priscila's forehead?
qa.a: Mummy Jana's hand was on Priscila's forehead.

qa.q: How did Priscila feel as Mummy stroked her hair?
qa.a: Priscila felt small, warm and safe. Curling up against Mummy's side and closing her eyes show that she trusted her.

qa.q: What did Jana do that showed care for her sick child?
qa.a: Jana sat close, spoke softly, hummed, and told Priscila she could rest. If the fever keeps going or worries her, she can check with the doctor. 🤍

qa.q: How might Jana feel as she sits with Priscila?
qa.a: Jana probably feels concerned and tender. She stays close and quiet so her daughter knows she is loved even when weak.

grounding: A child with a fever is held by her mother and feels small, warm and safe, learning she can be weak and still loved.

passage: In the clinic in Accra, Kwame gripped the edge of the chair. His heart thumped as he saw the little needle on the tray. Last time, someone had said, "It won't hurt at all," and it had. His eyes filled up and he began to cry. Dr Rania knelt down. "I'll tell you the truth, Kwame. It will pinch for a second, and I am here with you." Kwame sobbed but held out his arm. Dr Rania counted out loud. It pinched, and it was over. She said, "You were brave to stay."

qa.q: Where was Kwame when he saw the needle?
qa.a: Kwame was at a clinic in Accra.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling as he looked at the needle?
qa.a: Kwame was scared and remembered a time it hurt after someone said it wouldn't. His thumping heart and tears show his fear.

qa.q: Why was Dr Rania's way of talking to Kwame wise?
qa.a: Dr Rania told the truth, that it would pinch for a second, and stayed with him. Saying it won't hurt makes the next visit harder because he stops trusting.

qa.q: How might Kwame's trust in adults change after this visit?
qa.a: Kwame may trust Dr Rania more because what she said matched what happened. Next time he may still be scared but feel less alone.

grounding: A child cries at the sight of a needle and heart thumps, and a doctor tells the truth that it will pinch for a second and stays, unlike a lie that makes the next visit harder.
